utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, would you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. President. Case IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Prlic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Registrar. On this Monday when we're taking up our work again, I'd like to greet all the people in the courtroom, the representatives of the Prosecution, the Defence counsel, the accused, and all the other personnel and staff assisting us in the performance of our duty. Since this is a season of greeting, I should like to express my greetings and best wishes to everyone for this year and, of course, wishing you good health, which is always the most important thing, and I hope everybody's health will be good this year. And I hope that we'll be able to carry on our work in the best possible conditions. I'd also like to say that I hope that we shall have serenity, a calmness in our courtroom proceedings, because justice the process of justice is best served in a serene atmosphere. So I should like to say that to all of you and that our deliberations should be characterised by calmness and serenity it. I know that sometimes there are situations where this is not possible because of misunderstandings amongst us, but we have been helped up by a former judge, an American judge who was the chief judge of the American military court, and he is a foremost man in the legal profession. I'd like to prevail upon you all to meet him, and I'm sure that he will be able to help you with any problems, as will the legal assistants in our courtroom today, which might help us avoid any misunderstandings that might arise. I would also like to indicate that we have a series of decisions that we reached in the meantime, and one with respect to the exhibits, and this is a decision that was given on the 13th of December, 2006, and in order to summarise, I'd like to tell you that once we have heard a witness's testimony, when one of the parties asks for the tendering into evidence of an exhibit, they should provide a written list asking that these documents be admitted, and this should be done, at the latest, on the day that follows the conclusion of the witness's testimony. Taking the case of the last witness, the Prosecution and the Defence will have to tender the list at the latest by tomorrow, for instance, before the start of the hearing, and the written list must be submitted to the registrar and to the legal officer before the hearing starts. If there are any objections on either side, from either of the parties, as we have already stated in the decision, then these objections should be made in writing before the beginning of the first day after day two. So if we take the case that we took a moment ago, tomorrow at the latest you can ask for the tendering of the documents. If there are any objections, then the objection also have to be filed at the latest by Wednesday, for example, before we start the proceedings. Now, if there is a reply to the objections, then you will have an additional day to make this response. And after that, you will be given an IC number or, rather, the exhibit will be given an IC number by our registrar. I had should like to tell you that for the moment we have on standby two witnesses, and I should like to say that we -- documents have still not been accorded IC numbers. It is Witness CO, and the other witness is Kajmovic. So you will have to let us know quickly what lists you have with respect to those two witnesses. Now, as far as the witness we're going to hear today is concerned, we have envisaged two days for his testimony, today and tomorrow, so the list for that witness can be filed on Wednesday at this earliest, because we have two days of testimony in court. So that is what I wanted to let you know. I should also like to say now that Judge Trechsel isn't with us today because, for reasons of protocol, tomorrow he will be received by the Queen of the Netherlands, and therefore he is not be able to be here today, and he felt that it was no -- that good assisting today if he wasn't able to come tomorrow. So he has asked to be excused, and we shall be working in his absence. I should also like to tell you that Judge Mindua, who is here us here today, has been named, appointed member of the -- in the Dragomir Milosevic case. So our colleague Judge Mindua will also be taking part in two trials at the same time, two proceedings. So if he's with us in the morning, that means that in the afternoon he will be in the Dragomir Milosevic trial and vice versa. So that -- those are -- that is the information that I wanted to given you. I should like us to go into private session for a few moments. Mr. Registrar, would you do what is necessary.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're currently in open session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Sir, we are now in open session, so you can be heard outside the courtroom, and I would request you to be very careful in giving any information from which you could be identified. Also, be very careful if you do mention names not to mention what your relationship was. If that's required, we will go back into private session. So, sir, dealing -- or looking at Stolac and the composition of Stolac prior to the war, as to the town of Stolac, how was the -- what was the composition of the inhabitants of the town of Stolac around the first part of -- the 1990s?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have no precise information, but I know that they were for the most part Bosniaks. They called themselves Muslims at that time. There were also Serbs and about the same number of Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Could you give the Court any idea of the percentage, perhaps?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There could have been between 70 and 80 per cent Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: What about the rest of the municipality of Stolac? Could you give the Court an indication of the population and composition?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the other part of the municipality the composition was different. The number of Croats was significantly higher than the average for Stolac town, but I really don't know the percentages.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: During the 1990 elections, of which group were there the most voters?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Which nation? Which group do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Which voting bloc, looking at ethnicity, Croats, Bosniaks, or Serbs, had the most voters during that election?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In my estimate, as for elections themselves and the turnout, Croats had the highest turnout and the best results.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: But without looking at the results at this stage, physically speaking do you know which group had the most voters who would have been able to vote?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Muslims, that is Bosniaks.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Sir, when was the -- or, rather, looking at the Party for Democratic Action, who could become members of this party?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Anybody could have become a member, but as a rule they were Muslims, that is Bosniaks.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: During the 1990 municipal elections in Stolac, apart from the SDA which were the other major parties which participated in the election?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: HDZ, SDA, SDP, and perhaps one or two less important parties.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Is it correct that the HDZ represented essentially the Croats in the party?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Whom did the SDS represent?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: And the SDP?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is difficult to explain, but in my opinion the formerly undecided voted for the SDP, most of them Bosniaks.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: What was the outcome of the election in 1990 in Stolac municipality?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What I know for certain is that the HDZ won the greatest number of seats in the Municipal Assembly, followed by the SDA, followed by the SDS, and lastly the SDP. Other minor parties I don't know about.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: How many more seats did the HDZ have than the SDA?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can say with great certainty that at least one seat more was won by them than the SDA.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, just one point of clarification of a political nature. From what I understood, you told us that in Stolac there was a great number of Muslim electors, and according to the results of these elections, according what you say, the HDZ won a majority. Does this mean that a great number of Muslim people voted in favour of the HDZ?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So how can you explain this? How can you explain that the HDZ had the highest number of votes and had more votes than the SDA?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I can explain that in two ways. First, Croats had good organisation and a high turnout in the elections. As for Bosniaks or Muslims as they were called then, I know that a certain number of them, and not a small number at that, did not turn out at all. Another segment voted for the SDP candidates, so that it was only logical that the SDA failed to win the greatest number of seats in the Municipal Assembly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for this clarification.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Sir, the religious figures within Stolac municipality, to your knowledge did any of them have any influence or exert any influence over the electorate in the run-up to the election?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From what I know, you could say about all the three parties that they had influence. Some were less, some were more.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, based on the election result -- sorry. Based on the election results where the HDZ therefore had at least one more seat than the SDA, what did this mean in actual terms for the governance or how the local government was thereafter constituted?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's correct, and it was customary that the party who won the greatest number of seats had the greatest rights to appoint their people to various positions in the government and in the authorities generally.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Who became the mayor of Stolac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Zeljko Raguz.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: And from which party or group was he?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: HDZ.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: And what about the chief of police? Who was he and from what grouping was he?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. Pero Raguz, HDZ.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, turning it to April 1992. The Court has already heard that Stolac, the municipality, was occupied by Serb forces at that time. Is that correct, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: The Court has also previously heard that the Croat population of Stolac left the municipality. Is -- do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know a bit about those events.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, from what you know, the movement of the Croats away from the municipality, the population, was that spontaneous or organised in some way?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure whether it's the one or the other way, but I'm certain that it was because of the great danger from the Serbs' advance.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: What about you? Did you remain in Stolac during that period?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: And what about the other Bosniaks inhabitants?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They stayed for the most part.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you allow me to interrupt. I'm trying to understand the following: Why is it when the Serbs about to occupy Stolac the Croats leave and the Muslims remain? What kind of explanation can you give us for this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, there is a number of possible explanations for these events. One of those that I favour is that Bosniaks had no choice. They didn't know where to go, where they should go. And second, although it was strange for those times and the circumstances, but they thought naively that nothing would happen to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, sir, during the occupation and after the Croats had left, members of the SDS party in Stolac, Serbs, did they make any proposals to the SDA party and its membership?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What I know, and I took part in some of those talks, is that they insisted that we accept and get involved in the organisation of the so-called autonomous province of Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: And what was this Serb autonomous region for Herzegovina, very briefly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It covered several municipalities with predominant or majority Serb population, and it was created by the SDS. It was a creature of the SDS whereby the existence of Bosnia and Herzegovina would have been completely denied.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Did the SDA accept these proposals by the SDS?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. Not as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Do you know why not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: First of all, we Bosniaks at the time were convinced that we should respect the internationally recognised Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, its constitution and its laws, and that was our sole option.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, the Serb forces left the municipality of Stolac in June, 1992. Was this pursuant to any fights or battles with any other military groups?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What I know happened is this: That it happened in a short period of time, along with artillery firing. And as far as I know, the -- there was no infantry confrontation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: When the Serb forces left, were they replaced by any other forces?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, because Bosniaks had no organised military units. The parts that were left by Serbs were taken over by forces of the Croatian army and some forces that I met for the first time then, the HVO, as well as members of the HOS.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: How did -- how do you know that these forces that you encountered were either HV, HVO, or HOS?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have to confess that I found them difficult to distinguish at the beginning, but they were in camouflage uniforms. On their left or right arm, I can't remember, they had insignia, whereas HOS soldiers had distinctly black uniforms, something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: And just to clarify, the camouflage uniforms, were they worn by the HV and HVO soldiers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Were those camouflage uniforms to you either the same or different from each other?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You could say they were the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Apart from the patches that you saw and later came to distinguish -- distinguish between, did you or any other people, Bosniaks in the municipality, find out through any other means that some of these soldiers were members of the HV?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were more familiar with the term "Home Guard Corps," ZNG. And as far as I remember, some of the inhabitants of Stolac municipality of Croat ethnicity belonged to those military units.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: At that stage when the Croat forces entered, was there any objection from the Bosniaks that HV forces were also present?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, on the contrary. I have to say that their coming was like liberation from Serb occupation, and we didn't view it otherwise at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Up to where, regarding Stolac municipality, did the Serb forces occupy the municipality?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The date of withdrawal was between the 10th and the 20th July. Maybe the 14th or the 17th. I'm not sure. 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Sorry, I think my question was not formulated properly. What I actually meant, geographically up to what line did the Croat forces occupy the municipality?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The line where the Serb forces stopped is just above Stolac, overlooking Stolac. You could identify it with the historically known border of the entity known as Banovina, from the Second World War.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Did the Croats at any stage subsequently cross that line and occupy more territory?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't think so, and I don't think they wanted to.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, you already mentioned that the Bosniaks had no military organisation of their own. In the first few weeks after the -- let's call it liberation of Stolac, did the Bosniaks try to establish a Territorial Defence in Stolac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. They first gathered as a staff of the Territorial Defence in a village called Borojevici near Stolac, but as for their activities, I really doesn't know any details.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: To your knowledge, was a Territorial Defence successfully established within Stolac for the Bosniaks?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: What other option was available during that period for Bosniaks to join any defence organisation in Stolac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. At that time it was natural to join or affiliate with any units, any formations that offered resistance to the Serb aggression, because we expected a counter-attack from the Serbs whereby they would return to the area of Stolac and Capljina municipalities.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: And in practice during those first few weeks after the liberation, which force did the local Bosniaks join?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: HVO forces and the Croatian army.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: The Croatian army, do you know which part of the Croatian a army or which brigade or regiment was joined?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know for a fact that they were members of the 116th Brigade of HVO from Metkovici, or based in Metkovici.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Just for the record, could we clarify. The 116th Brigade, was that of the HV or the HVO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, if we could move into private session at this stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before moving into private session, one point of clarification, sir. You are telling us that the Serbs left Stolac between the 10th and the 20th of July, 1992. You said that Stolac was liberated by three entities. You said HOS, HVO, and the HV. I understand that you were an eyewitness because you were present. As far as you remember, the liberation of Stolac by these three entities or these three groups, did you feel at the time that these three groups were commanded by one single entity, or were these groups commanded by different people? What is your feeling about this? What do you feel? What was your feeling at the time about these liberators?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I really couldn't know at that time about the various levels of command over these units, but I could confirm that I had the feeling that the actions of the HVO and the Croatian army were harmonised, coordinated. I don't know about the HOS.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, to try to understand matters more clearly, from what I understood, before the occupation by the Serbs (redacted)

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Your Honour, before the witness answers that question, if I can draw Your Honour's attention to the question itself and certain matters that could be possibly better dealt with in private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, you are quite right, Mr. Murphy. We shall move back into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Registrar, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're in open session, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Witness, we're now in open session, so be careful in divulging information which may identify you. Now, the Crisis Staff that was established in -- in Stolac municipality, how did their banking affairs work?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Banking affairs in Stolac municipality were non-existent. You couldn't conduct any banking affairs at all in whatever shape or form. The only possibility was that this could be done in Metkovici, and Metkovici in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: And what arrangements were in place in order to transact or do financial transactions at this bank; to withdraw money, for instance, for the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was the possibility of opening a bank account in one of the banks or branches, and that the representatives of the Crisis Staff have the right to dispose of the money on that account.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Based on the 50/50 composition of the Crisis Staff, did this also have an influence in how banking transactions were done or how money was withdrawn?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At the beginning everything was very proper, and then as time went by two Bosniaks who had the right to withdraw money and had had -- on the basis of their signatures lost that right because they used some money. And the money that was on the account was exclusively at the disposal of two Croats, and their signatures were registered in the bank as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Is it correct that at one stage the Crisis Staff moved 180 tonnes of tobacco for safe storage in Metkovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: And what happened to this tobacco?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know. Especially since cooperation had ceased with the HDZ, and because I, before arrested and taken to camp, had very restricted movements in the Stolac, Dubrava, and Capljina area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Was any of this tobacco sold, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know for certain that a truckload was sold, perhaps seven tonnes of tobacco, to the Zagreb tobacco factory.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: And what happened to the funds which were received for this sale, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Those funds were placed in a joint account that was opened in one of the Metkovici banks.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Do you know whether this -- whether these funds were used for the -- for both the benefit of Bosniaks and Croats within the municipality?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I know, at the beginning everything was in proper order.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I did not react thus far, but I'd like to ask my learned colleague to put the questions in the way they should be put and not be leading questions. Perhaps it can speed up the process, but as far as I know, one should not ask questions in that form.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you. I've taken note, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Witness, the -- let's move on to another topic. You've described the establishment of a Crisis Staff in the municipality, and that deals with the civilian side of affairs. What about the military side? Was there ever talk of cooperation between Croats and Bosniaks on the military field or military area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. As the Bosniaks were not successful in organising units of the Territorial Defence for Stolac municipality - they were supposed to be established pursuant to the laws of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina - all that was left to do was to join up with the Croats and organise them that way, and so reinforce defence against a possible Serb aggression.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Sorry. Initially when such cooperation was set up, did Croat soldiers and Bosniak soldiers appear together on the front lines or did they share the front lines, or did they have separate front lines towards the Serb positions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At the very beginning they were separate. However, in a short space of time they became mixed so that there was no clear-cut distinction for the most part. There was no small Croatian or Bosniak military unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: When these units became mixed, did they also then have a -- or how was the command structured?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In Stolac we had a forward command post for Stolac.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Sorry, may I interrupt you. Before we come to that, I'd like to ask about the physical composition of the units that -- that were in existence. First of all, just talking about the -- before the command of the units themselves.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The HVO units had their own command, and for the most part those units were made up of Croats. A smaller number of units with fewer soldiers were members of the TO, the Territorial Defence, but they did not have some higher level of organisation and establishment and combat readiness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Let's move on, then, to the forward command post or the IZM. And when we come to certain aspects of it I will ask to go into closed session or private session. When was this IZM established?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I can't remember the date when it comes to the actual time, but I do know that it was soon after this mixture of military units, when they became mixed, and that could have been sometime towards the end of June and beginning of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: These mixed military units, what did they consist of, brigades, battalions, companies?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The forward command post, as the highest military organ in Stolac municipality, was composed of two military formations, two battalions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: And who was the overall commander of these two battalions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The commander of the forward command post was Pavlovic. I can't remember his first name now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: And the individual -- two composing battalions or units, how -- how were they commanded? And here I'm referring to the composition in terms of ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When the mixed units were established, I wasn't present myself but somebody at some point had agreed that the commander of the two formations be a Croat. In this case it was Bozo Pavlovic, and that his deputy should be Edo Obradovic, and that the commanders of one battalion should take turns. If the battalion commander was a Croat, his deputy was a Bosniak, and vice versa.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: The -- these two units, to which military organisation did they belong?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They belonged to the Knez Domagoj Brigade, whose headquarters was in Capljina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: The Knez Domagoj Brigade, is that correct that that is an HVO brigade?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Do you know who the overall commander of the Knez Domagoj Brigade was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do, and I met him too. It was Mr. Obradovic, Nedjeljko Obradovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, just before moving into private session again, could you perhaps sum up to the Court the difference between the Crisis Staff and the IZM, their areas of responsibility?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: First of all, the forward command post usually as a rule had military tasks and assignments. It was their duty to see to the mobilisation of manpower, the organisation and material resources. And the Crisis Staff had the duty to see to the needs of the population. Health care, Red Cross organisation, that kind of thing. Civilian protection --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, if we may move into private session again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, registrar, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Sir, if we can briefly look at the establishment of the Bregava Brigade. Do you know when the Bregava -- ABiH Bregava Brigade was established?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't remember the date, although there was a decree establishing it issued by the government of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: The Bregava Brigade, what was it composed of, or who became members of it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Bregava Brigade was made up primarily of Bosniaks who were not engaged in HVO units of Stolac.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Where was this brigade established physically?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The brigade was set up in a part of Mostar town known as south -- southern camp housing the barracks of the former JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Is there a reason why it was not set up in Stolac physically?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From what I know and from what I've heard, it was not possible to do it in Stolac municipality, in any part of Stolac municipality, because the HVO units were opposed to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: The IZM or forward command post, when the Bregava Brigade was established, do you know what their general view towards it was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At one of those meetings that I attended at the forward command post there was talk about the problems that may arise should the unit be located in Stolac municipality. Some of the attendees held a very negative position concerning the establishment of such a unit and its deployment in the HVO's area of responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: The attendees at that meeting and without giving particulars of their identities, to which group did these people belong, if any?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were mostly officers of that forward command post, but it's also possible that some member or members of the Knez Domagoj Brigade were also present.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Those opposing, were they Bosniaks, Croats, or both?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, in a moment we -- I'll ask us to move back into private session to deal with specific aspects regarding the next topic, but before we go into private session, who was Andjelko Markovic in 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Andjelko Markovic was the first president of the HDZ of Stolac municipality. At one point during a certain period he did not discharge his functions in the HDZ, for reasons that I ignore, and his deputy, as far as I know, was Mr. Niko Kuzman. Andjelko Markovic returned to his post of president of the HDZ in 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: When he returned to his post in 1993, can you give the Court an idea as to what time of the year it was, at what stage?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It could have been sometime in October, perhaps November, 1992, but I really can't be sure. One thing is certain, though. He did act as the president of the HDZ in 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, sir, before moving to the private session, up until the point where Andjelko Markovic returned in October or November 1992, to your knowledge, how was the cooperation between Bosniaks and Croats in both the forward command post, the IZM, and the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I could qualify it briefly as a solid and good cooperation. My personal cooperation was the strongest with Mr. Zeljko Raguz.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, when Mr. Andjelko Markovic returned, did this good, solid cooperation continue? And just a brief answer, because then we'll move into private session for details.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: With the coming of Andjelko Markovic things changed a lot, in my opinion for the worse. Andjelko Markovic offered us, among other things, to sign certain documents that --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Could I interrupt you there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- clearly showed in the heading --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: If we may move back into private session, Your Honour, for ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're in each session, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, sir, looking at the situation in Stolac during 1992, after the Serbian occupation and then going through into 1993, were schools functioning in Stolac municipality?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, not a single one.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: What was done in order to see to the schooling of the children in the municipality?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Most of the refugees from Stolac municipality were accommodated in the Neretva River valley: Capljina, Visici, and the surrounding parts. But there were some in Makarska and other parts of the Adriatic coast. Now, as far as the population was concerned, which stayed in Stolac municipality and Capljina, the possibility of having education was only in Capljina. That was the only place that they could go to school in. And to a certain extent in Mostar as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, just to get things clear, when the Serbs took control of Stolac were the schools working? Did they continue to function regardless of the fact that the Croats had left? And during the Serb occupation, were the schools functioning?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, yes. Since the Serbs occupied the area in April, (redacted)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So the tuition was interrupted and brought to an end. When was that? What month?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it could have even been before June. They might have ended the school year before June.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When the Serbs left, was it impossible to have the schools open up in September, October, 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, that was unthinkable because the buildings themselves, the premises, because they were shelled every day and frequently were completely destroyed. The electric power system, the water supply system, that had all been destroyed and all the other utilities in town ceased to function. The population moved out or was moved out to the areas I mentioned earlier on, so that all for intents and purposes in Stolac life had come to a standstill or was going on in its minimum form with a great deal of risk involved because, as I say, there was shelling every day, shelling by the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honour, I notice in the transcript on page 53, line 11, we're in open session and something slipped through that we will need to redact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What exactly?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, there's a reference to the function that the witness performed, which may identify him, his career.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't see exactly when we mentioned his functions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: It's just gone off.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We'll look into that. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, sir, moving back to the HVO in Stolac, which continued making decisions without the Bosniaks, I would like to show you an exhibit, 01234.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: And with the assistance of the usher, if I could show the hard-copy version to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: It's in the first bundle of documents. It's the one you have on top, and it's 1234.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I know that the witness wears glasses. I wonder if the witness has his glasses with him.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry. Yes. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, sir, I'll deal with the header of this document in a moment, but this document is one that you have seen before. I showed it to you yesterday. It's signed by Dr. Nedjeljko Obradovic, and it's a decision to impose a curfew on the 20th of January, 1993. Now, my first question to you is: If you look at Article 6 of this document, there's reference to the departments who are authorised being the Stolac police station and the military police. At this stage, to your knowledge, were these two authorities composed still -- still of mixed composition, Bosniak and Croat, or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were not mixed. Police and armed forces were composed solely of Croats.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I would just like to remind us that in response to one of the previous questions the witness said that they gave instructions to Muslims in the civilian police force to leave the police force. I would just like that recommendation to be borne in mind when we hear answers like this.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, might I just add to my learned lead counsel's comments that counsel asked -- mentioned to the witness that he'd been shown this document yesterday. What would also be pertinent would be to establish at the very beginning whether the witness had ever seen the document before.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Sir, this document, prior to yesterday, had you ever seen this document before or did you know about this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Mm-hmm. And how did you know about it or -- without revealing details which can identify you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I had occasion to get hold of documents in a variety of ways simply because they were not confidential. They were public documents. I cannot specify at this moment in which particular way I had occasion to see this document. These were not secret documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, sir, if you look at the preamble of this document, it says: "Based on Article 4, paragraph 2 of the decision," and then it refers to a decision and an Official Gazette. Do you know which laws or gazette this refers to, which authorities, laws, or gazette?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, if we look at the header of this document, there indeed you have a Croatian coat of arms, and then logo as well, but just above that appears the words "Republika Bosna Hercegovina. "Without saying what role you had with this but what is the significance of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina being or appearing in the header?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, is this a question to the witness that's going to elicit some knowledge from the witness, in which case it's legitimate, or is it designed to elicit some opinion or some sort of legal view, in which case it's not a legitimate question? We do need to be very clear about that distinction.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, the witness will make this clear and perhaps it's best to move into private session then at this stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's move into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're back in open session, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, sir, if you can turn to document 5717 in your document bundle. It's Exhibit 05717. It's the second last document. That's correct now. Now, is it correct that this is a media article that you supplied or provided to the Office of the Prosecutor when you were first interviewed by them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, sir, this article which appeared in Slobodna Dalmacija on the 7th of October, 1993, contains an interview with Andjelko Markovic. Is that Andjelko Markovic's picture on -- on the first page of the article?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, I'd like to refer you to column 1, and just before the reference to Knez Domagoj, in the translated version -- it's on the second page of the translated version, right at the top. The interviewer has asked a question, "How many people have returned to Stolac," and the article says, "Expelled Croats from Kakanj and Kraljeva Sutjeska have arrived in Stolac together with returnees. We have put about 3.000 of them on the Dubrava plateau on the town of Stolac itself." My question, sir, is does this actually reflect what happened on the ground in Stolac or had happened by October, 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In October, 1993, we did not have access to the area. The male Bosniaks were all in camps, or mostly all of them. And I was in a camp, too, in one of the camps. So as far as the situation on the ground is concerned in Stolac and Capljina municipality, I don't know what it was like.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: According to --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: However --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: If I may interrupt. According to your knowledge, when there is talk about returnees in Stolac in October, does that include Bosniaks?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, in no case.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: If I can refer you to the second column of the article, right in the middle. And this is where the question is asked: "Croats emphasise that they were the majority population in Stolac before the war." Do you have that?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: In the translated version, Your Honours, it is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: It's also on page -- page 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Andjelko Markovic is reported as saying in this regard: "The first multi-party elections illustrated who Stolac belongs to." What comment do you have on that? He's obviously, I think, referring to the election of 1990.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I emphasised earlier on, most of the Bosniaks lived in the town of Stolac itself, and fewer people lived in the surrounding villages. Now, I got this information earlier on from a programme that was on television that I happened to see, but they weren't as precise as this. It is true that in parts of the municipality outside town this information could be fairly correct as applying to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: If I can refer you to one more part, and that is in column three, just beneath the section which states, "Going to Tudjman."

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: And in the translated version, Your Honours, it is on page 3 of the translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, the question that the -- that was posed during the interview is, "Why do Muslims particularly insist on getting Stolac," to which Markovic appears to give two reasons. One says: "Strategic. They need it for access to the sea," which is at the beginning of his response. And about a third of the way down he says: "In the second place, it is the hometown of the majority of the SDA leadership." In your view how accurate is this response or ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, judging by what I know, some of the people were -- from Stolac were active in the SDA party, in the Main Board, or in the Presidency of the party in Sarajevo. But that they were fundamentalists, I can't agree with that, with that observation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: And what about the contention that Muslims insist on getting Stolac because they need access to the sea?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kruger, put your question again.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: What about the contention, Witness, that Muslims particularly insist on getting Stolac because they need it for access to the sea?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What I know is this: At the time there was the prevalent view that the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina was under an embargo and that possibly the arrival of the BH army to Stolac and Neum would be -- would allow the arming of the units of the BH army. So that was the opinion that was held, as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: But was it at all a question that the Muslims insist on getting Stolac? What is meant by this? Was it a relevant question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know. I can't say for sure. I can't be sure what Mr. Markovic meant by saying that, but the fact remains that they or he and his policies were geared towards not allowing Bosniaks to spend time on the territory of Stolac municipality and, among others, in order to achieve this goal that he states, the goal that he stipulates in this part of the article.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Sir, this article, the views expressed by Andjelko Markovic in this article, did they at all surprise you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. Especially not after the talks I had as a camp inmate with representatives of the investigating organs in the camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, if I can refer you to another document, and this is exhibit --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment. Before we move on to another document, Witness, I have a follow-up question to ask you. In page 63, lines 12 and 13, you said the following: You said that all the Muslim men were in camps, and then you added that, "I, too, was in a camp," you say. How do you explain the fact that your compatriots were put in camps? What in your opinion led up to this, led them to be placed in camps? And most particularly your own situation. How were you yourself -- how did you yourself end up in a camp? Can you give us some explanations about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have a number of explanations to give you with more or less arguments to support them, but I'll try and focus on what was the subject of discussion between myself as a camp inmate and an investigator in the Dretelj camp, or interrogator. The interrogator there asked -- or, rather, accused me personally of the following: By not abiding by the laws of Herceg-Bosna that I had --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment, please. As we're in open session, if you're going to say anything that might identify you, we could perhaps move into private session. Perhaps that would be advisable. So, Mr. Registrar, let's move back into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 9th day of January, 2007, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 7.00 p.m.,
